items.description: This video demonstrates the training and testing processes of the proposed task attention-based residual reinforcement learning method for robotic assembly tasks. Key Points Demonstrated in the Video: 1. **Training Process**: The video shows the initial training phase where the model is trained at a fixed position. During this phase, large deviations can be observed as the actuator approaches the assembly point. These deviations, which are in the centimeter range, are effectively corrected by the model, which successfully aligns the peg with the hole that has a clearance of only 0.1 mm. 2. **Testing Process**: The video illustrates the robustness of the trained model in different test scenarios. The task board is randomly positioned within the workspace, and the surrounding environment is dynamically adjusted to introduce disturbances. Despite these challenges, the model quickly adjusts the end-effector position and orientation, achieving successful insertion in various unstructured environments. The video serves to provide readers with a clear and visual representation of the experiment, complementing the written content of the paper by showcasing the model's ability to overcome errors and disturbances during real-world assembly tasks.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Driven by demands for assembly quality and efficiency, robotic assembly has become a cornerstone of autonomous industrial systems. However, contact-rich assembly tasks are constrained by challenges in reliability, data efficiency, and generalization, making conventional position control insufficient for stability and robustness in real-world autonomous production lines. Although compliant control, visuo-tactile sensor fusion, and imitation learning have emerged as enablers of adaptive robotic behavior, the existing literature lacks a systematic review encompassing task modeling, policy generalization, and standardized evaluation. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the imitation learning application framework for robotic assembly, organized around three core dimensions: reliability, efficiency, and adaptability, which constitute fundamental requirements for industrial deployment: predictable physical interaction, cost-effective, and robust adaptation to product variants and environmental changes. To establish a foundation for understanding data-driven capabilities and limitations, we describe the physical components of an assembly system, including demonstration modalities, hardware topology, and multimodal perception. Building on this, we trace algorithmic evolution from structured movement primitives to generative policies, proposing a selection methodology to guide integrated manufacturing deployment. Furthermore, this review surveys prevailing benchmarks and data ecosystems; to overcome the limitations of current evaluation metrics that prioritize outcomes over processes, we propose a standardized evaluation protocol. This protocol enables unified quantitative diagnostics across four dimensions: task accomplishment, contact quality, generalization robustness, and system resilience. Finally, the bottlenecks impeding the transition of robotic assembly from lab to autonomous industrial deployment are identified, followed by a discussion of prospective research frontiers.</jats:p>
